title: Combat Search and Rescue Project
description: Package about the Air Force Combat Search and Rescue Project. Produced by Senior Airman Brian Economides.

transcript.text: So I knew at that point when they brought all that out there to carry to their guys that
this was going to be a serious mission.
It's probably one of the best jobs out there.
Next thing you know over the radio is we hear Scramble.
At that time both crews are screwing as fast as they can and get these vehicles.
My job there I'm writing down Nine Line and that Nine Line is very important information
where we're going, who are picking up, injuries, threats in the area, all information needed
so that we can get out there and do the job.
We drive up to the aircraft, we're jumping there, I jump on radio right away.
One of my jobs as the guner out there is not just to man the guns to make sure they're
working appropriately but I'm talking back here to the command center getting information
on new updates, threats in the area, stuff like that, finding out coordinating with them,
what we got to do and we got to do what kind of stuff.
So I'm constantly on the radio talking to them while I'm out there scanning and if need
be assisting the medical team or the preachers in the back with their gear or at the time
but with a pick up patient up, picking up patient up.
We get out there, get settled in and we're taking off from Scramble within five to six
minutes and routes anywhere.
Most of our missions are under an hour and we're getting the patients back here in the
treatment and they're living.
Speed is key.
There's something called the golden hour.
So from the time of injury to the time of treatment a typical person has about an hour
to survive.
So we try to get out there and pick that person up and bring him back within that hour.
It's one of the most challenging yet rewarding missions.
